steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The sea had stolen many things from Elias Finch over the years—his appetite for crowded rooms, the color from half his beard, his wife—and yet it had never managed to steal his devotion. Every evening, just before dusk, he climbed the 137 iron-tipped steps of Warden’s Point Lighthouse, carrying a brass oil can in one hand and a battered journal in the other. He tended the great lantern, polished the fresnel glass, trimmed the wick, and then sat at the gallery railing to wait for the first star.

Tonight, the sky felt taut, as though stitched too tightly across the horizon. Gulls wheeled in uneasy circles, and the wind tasted like copper. Elias thumbed open his journal, found an empty page, and, with the stub of a pencil, wrote:

Storm coming. No forecast on the radio, but the sea is speaking.

He had learned long ago to trust the sea’s grammar. When the swells formed crooked question marks and the clouds bunched like knuckles, questions turned to blows soon after.

By twilight the gale arrived, sudden and muscular. Waves rose like black scaffolding, hammering the cliff face. The lighthouse groaned. The lantern’s beam made frantic sweeps across the water, smearing white across the dark.

Elias tightened the storm shutters, then stumbled back to the service room, heart jackhammering. On the floor, among coils of rope and salt-crusted boots, the radio crackled to life.

“Mayday… Cutter Gulliver… bearings lost… engine failure…”

He knelt, pressed the transmitter. “Gulliver, this is Warden’s Point Light. Keep your bow to the wind. I have you in sight.”

“Lightkeeper,” a strained voice replied, “we don’t see you. Fog’s thick. Fuel’s gone.”

Elias stood, eyes narrowing. Fog? But the lantern was blazing like a captive star. He raced up the last spiral of stairs and burst onto the lantern level. The fresnel glass shone, bright as ever. Yet beyond the panes, the beam faltered, choking on swirls of vapor that seemed to generate themselves, wheeling inwards, swallowing the light.

Elias pressed his palm to the glass. The cold bled through. And then he saw it: an immense shape beneath the waves, circling, luminous veins pulsing a sickly blue. Not a storm, but a thing—calling mist to itself, feeding on fear, bending the sea into new sentences of ruin.

He’d heard the legends—the Drowned Oracle, that leviathan of fog and static. Sailors said it sought silence, devouring every light that dared speak to the night.

Elias glanced once at the oil can, half empty, then at his journal, words still drying. If the Oracle wanted silence, he would give it a deafening answer.

He emptied the remaining oil onto the lantern platform, struck a match, and watched flame mingle with the lamp’s fire until the chamber roared white-hot. Glass fissured; metal shrieked.

Below, in the maelstrom, the Oracle howled—a low, continental groan. The fog shredded. The lighthouse blazed like a sunrise, and its beam speared the dark, undammed at last.

Seconds later, the radio sputtered: “We see you! Holding course!”

Elias exhaled, shoulders sagging. He managed to douse the excess fire before it consumed the tower, but not before it left soot tattoos on the walls and a gentle tremor in his bones.

When morning came, the sea smoothed itself into placid innocence. The Cutter Gulliver anchored safely in the cove, crew waving gratitude up the cliff.

Elias reopened his journal, charcoal flakes falling from his cuffs.

Fog wasn’t weather, he wrote. It was listening.

He closed the book, placed it beside the cracked lens, and faced the sea—ready, if silence dared return, to raise his voice again.
